label: Geometry of Time Series and Linear Systems
notes: Open the chapter. We apply information geometry to dynamic data and to the space of linear systems. The deck follows printed pages 115 through 132 and treats time series models, the manifold of stable linear systems, the spectral-density representation of the Fisher metric, and system identification recast as projection onto a model family.

label: Time Series Models
notes: Introduce stationary time series and the autoregressive and moving-average families. Each choice of model parameters defines a probability law on infinite sequences, so the collection of models is again a statistical manifold. The geometry developed for independent samples carries over once we use the asymptotic likelihood appropriate to stationary processes.

label: Manifold of Linear Systems
notes: Describe the space of stable linear systems as a manifold coordinatized by transfer-function parameters. Stability constrains the parameters to an open region, and the dually flat structure organizes this region. Points are systems, curves are deformations, and the same exponential and mixture coordinates reappear in the frequency domain representation of the process.

label: Spectral Fisher Metric
notes: Express the Fisher information metric for a stationary process through its spectral density. The metric becomes an integral over frequency comparing log-spectra, the natural inner product for stationary signals. This spectral form makes the geometry computable from power spectra and connects information geometry to classical signal processing and filter design.

label: System Identification
notes: Recast system identification as projecting the observed spectrum onto the model manifold using the spectral divergence. The estimated system is the closest model in the information sense, and the Pythagorean theorem again decomposes the approximation error. Model order selection appears as choosing the dimension of the manifold onto which we project.

label: Recap
notes: Close the chapter. Time series families form statistical manifolds, stable linear systems make a dually flat space, the Fisher metric has a clean spectral form, and identification is projection onto a model. The geometric program extends seamlessly from static distributions to dynamics, and Chapter 06 turns to multiterminal information theory.
